overview: East Polynesian voyagers established communities in Aotearoa around the thirteenth-century transition to the fourteenth. This early-period card follows settlement, food production and watercraft through named archaeological sites. Māori histories encompass distinct communities and traditions; this map label does not identify a single kingdom.

periods.title: Voyagers establish new communities
periods.summary: Early communities adapted fishing, tool-making and horticulture to Aotearoa. Wairau Bar preserves production debris and varied food remains; its early occupation is approximately dated, not a documented national founding.

periods.title: Watercraft and regional adaptation
periods.summary: The Anaweka canoe’s surviving hull preserves skilled woodworking and repair. Researchers place its last voyage around 1400, although the timber and caulking provide different dating evidence. Its form connects local materials with wider Polynesian boat-building traditions.

sections.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves

items.text: At Wairau Bar, unfinished adzes and stone-working waste record the shaping of argillite brought from the Nelson and D’Urville Island region. The concentration suggests organised production, potentially supplying other communities, rather than only occasional tool repair.

Wairau Bar fishing equipment adapts Polynesian designs to local materials, including moa bone and stone where tropical pearl shell was unavailable. Middens also contain fish, shellfish, birds, dogs and marine mammals. Early livelihoods drew on several resources.

Isotope analysis distinguishes childhood environments recorded in tooth enamel from later diets recorded in bone. Wairau Bar ancestors show differences in food and likely mobility; those signals do not identify a precise birthplace for every person or a uniform diet for the settlement.

Ornaments and equipment accompanied some Wairau Bar burials, including drilled moa eggs, worked teeth and adzes. These objects document distinctive treatment of the dead. They cannot, by themselves, establish a complete hierarchy of occupations or rank among the living.

sections.title: Growing food in a cooler environment

items.text: At Triangle Flat in Golden Bay/Mohua, planting pits dated to 1290 to 1385 contained microscopic starch interpreted as kūmara-like, alongside evidence attributed to taro and yam. The finding places horticultural experimentation within the early settlement period.

Triangle Flat lies within the customary jurisdiction of Manawhenua ki Mohua. Its garden evidence challenges the assumption that early southern settlers relied almost entirely on hunting and gathering after abandoning tropical crops. That conclusion concerns this investigated landscape, not every settlement.

A surviving canoe hull from Anaweka on the South Island’s northwest coast was shaped from native mataī wood. Internal ribs and a longitudinal stringer were carved into the hull, while lashing holes joined components. These features reveal construction knowledge beyond simply hollowing a log.

Additional holes beside damaged lashings show repairs to the Anaweka hull. Caulking helps date its final use to approximately 1400; older wood dates do not establish when the canoe was built. Researchers reconstruct the wider vessel from a surviving component.

A turtle carved in relief on the Anaweka hull resembles motifs in other Polynesian traditions. The researchers interpret it as evidence of cultural connections. It does not establish a uniquely identifiable departure island or the biography of the people aboard.

Local groups maintained their own authority and relationships through genealogy, mana and tapu. Exchange carried valued materials such as pounamu, obsidian and harakeke among communities. Shared practices coexisted with regional histories and changing social ties.

ending.text: The map’s 1530 endpoint is a change in coverage, not the disappearance of Māori. Colonial confiscations later dispossessed many communities, while iwi, hapū and whānau continued. The kōhanga reo movement, beginning in 1982, is one example of community-led language transmission across generations.
